1: Welcome the group. This is the first module in the US Training Programme and the one everything else hangs off. Frame it simply: the rest of the Playbook teaches you how to do the job; this session sets the standard for how we do it here.
2: Set the contract for the session.
3: The one-page view. Read the six out loud, then ask the room: which one do you think you are strongest at, and which one would your last manager say you need to work on? Take two or three answers, it warms people up and makes the next six slides personal. Keep each to around seven minutes.
4: Our markets, AI, data, energy, infrastructure, move every quarter, so the pitch that worked in January will be stale by June. Give a real example from the desk of someone who changed a template, outreach sequence or market map and it paid off. Then give two minutes for the prompt. Ask one or two people to share; capture good ideas on a flipchart and commit to trialling one as a team. Link forward: Business Development and Candidate modules both depend on bringing market intel to every conversation.
5: Use the “40 calls vs role placed” line to start a discussion about activity versus outcome, activity matters but only as a means to an outcome. Exercise: everyone names one stalled item, a job with no feedback, a candidate gone quiet, and a single action they will take before the end of the day. Ask two people to share, and follow up with them tomorrow.
6: Ask the room what a client actually buys from us, the answer is speed, access to talent they can’t reach, and advice. Good examples of an insight: salary movement for a role family, a competitor’s hiring push, candidate availability for a skill set, a realistic time-to-fill. Exercise: each person writes their opening insight for their next client call. Managers should check on Friday whether it was used.
7: We run several brands on one floor, Technology Perm, Evergreen and Contract. Cross-referrals between desks are some of the cheapest NFI we make: a Software Engineering candidate who mentions a hiring manager in energy is a lead for Evergreen. Exercise: everyone names one lead or candidate they could pass to another desk and to whom. Make the hand-offs happen before the end of the session if possible.
8: A simple structure for feedback: what I saw, the impact, what I’d like instead. Exercise: people write privately, no sharing names. Ask them to commit to a date for the conversation.
9: Explain leading versus lagging indicators. Lagging: NFI, placements. Leading: quality calls, client meetings booked, submissions, first interviews. You control the leading ones every day. Exercise: each person writes one weekly target (for example, [__] client meetings or [__] first interviews) agreed with their manager. Set the actual numbers per desk, this deck deliberately does not fix them.
10: Explain each term briefly for new starters. NFI = net fee income, the fee or margin we actually earn. Budget = the NFI target for your desk. Breakeven = the NFI a desk needs to cover its own cost. PPH = productivity per head, total NFI divided by headcount. Show where they can see their own numbers in the CRM or reporting pack. Exercise prompt: write your current NFI, your gap to budget and one action to close it, share with your manager this week.
11: If you have a current US org chart, put it up here or hand it out. Walk through the three brands, Evergreen, Technology Perm and Contract, and who leads each. Stress that escalating through your direct line isn’t bureaucracy; it keeps decisions fast and means your manager can actually help. Prompt: confirm your reporting line and write one thing you need from it to do your job well. Share it in your next 1:1. About 5 minutes.
12: Change the energy here, this is the why behind everything else. Share your own example first if you are comfortable doing so; it gives the room permission to be honest. Ask two or three volunteers what they are working toward outside work this year. Keep it personal and positive, no one has to share numbers. About 8 minutes.
13: Give everyone a card or a page. Keep it short, three lines is perfect. Walk the room during the reflect step and nudge people toward specific behaviours (“I’ll share one lead a week with another desk”) rather than vague ones (“be more of a team player”). Pairs read their standard to each other; the partner’s only job is to ask “how will you know you’ve done it?” Managers: collect a copy and revisit at the 30-day review.
14: Ask each person to circle the one action they will do first and tell the room. Managers should follow up on all five actions in the next weekly 1:1.
